passages.title: The Attic
passages.intro: Read the story below, then answer questions 1–6. Paragraphs are numbered.
passages.credit: Original story written for this practice test.
paragraphs: Great-Aunt Harriet's house smelled of beeswax and old books, and it was full of things Nell was not allowed to touch. There were glass-fronted cabinets of shells, a clock that chimed thirteen times at midnight, and a stuffed owl that regarded visitors with a disapproving, slightly cross-eyed stare.

'You may explore,' Great-Aunt Harriet announced on the first morning, 'provided you do not disturb anything.' Nell privately thought that exploring without disturbing anything was like swimming without getting wet.
For two days she was impeccably well-behaved. On the third day it rained, the kind of steady, grey rain that makes a house feel smaller, and her good intentions began to wear thin.

The attic stairs were narrow and complained loudly at every step. At the top, under a dusty sheet, Nell found a wooden box with a brass clasp. Inside, wrapped in tissue paper, lay a telescope – and a notebook filled with tiny, careful handwriting and drawings of stars.
'Ah,' said a voice behind her. Nell spun around, her face burning. Great-Aunt Harriet stood at the top of the stairs, and for a long, dreadful moment neither of them spoke.

Then the old woman crossed the room, lifted the telescope as gently as if it were a sleeping bird, and smiled for the first time since Nell had arrived. 'I was eleven when I made those drawings,' she said. 'I had quite forgotten. Tonight, if the clouds clear, I shall show you Saturn.'

passages.title: Cat's Eyes
passages.intro: Read the text below. Choose the best word to fill each of the 8 gaps (questions 7–14).
passages.credit: Original text written for this practice test.
passages.text:
Before electric lights, travelling at night was difficult and often dangerous. Roads were dark, and it was {1} to see holes, rocks or other travellers until it was too late.

In the 1930s an English inventor named Percy Shaw had an idea that would {2} improve road safety. Driving home one foggy night, he noticed his headlights {3} in the eyes of a cat by the side of the road. This gave him the idea for 'cat's eyes': small glass {4} set into the middle of the road that reflect light back towards drivers.

Shaw's invention was simple but {5}. Each cat's eye is fixed in a rubber case, so when a car drives over it, it is pushed down and wiped clean. During the Second World War, when street lights had to be switched off, cat's eyes {6} drivers to find their way safely. Today they are used on roads all over the world, and Shaw's idea is still {7} as one of the most {8} inventions of the twentieth century.

passages.title: From a Railway Carriage
passages.intro: Read the poem below, then answer questions 15–19. Lines are numbered. (brambles: prickly bushes with berries; tramp: a person with no home who travels on foot; lumping: moving heavily and clumsily.)
passages.credit: Robert Louis Stevenson, A Child's Garden of Verses, 1885. Public domain.
stanzas: Faster than fairies, faster than witches,
Bridges and houses, hedges and ditches;
And charging along like troops in a battle,
All through the meadows the horses and cattle:
All of the sights of the hill and the plain
Fly as thick as driving rain;
And ever again, in the wink of an eye,
Here is a child who clambers and scrambles,
All by himself and gathering brambles;
Here is a tramp who stands and gazes;
And there is the green for stringing the daisies!
Here is a cart run away in the road
Lumping along with man and load;
And here is a mill and there is a river:
Each a glimpse and gone for ever!

passages.title: An Idea That Stuck
passages.intro: Six sentences have been removed from the article. Choose the sentence (A–G) that best fits each gap (questions 20–25). There is one extra sentence you do not need.
passages.credit: Original article written for this practice test.
paragraphs: In 1941, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral went for a walk in the mountains with his dog. When they returned, both of them were covered in burrs, the prickly seed cases of a plant called burdock. [[1]]

Instead of simply pulling them off, de Mestral looked at the burrs under a microscope. [[2]] Fur and the loops in his woollen trousers caught on these hooks, which is how the plant spreads its seeds to new places.
De Mestral realised that the same idea could be used to join two pieces of fabric. [[3]] Making it work, however, was far from easy.

For years he experimented with different materials. Cotton wore out quickly, and many weavers thought his idea was ridiculous. [[4]] When this was heated, it formed tough little hooks that could be opened and closed thousands of times.

De Mestral patented his invention in 1955 and named it Velcro, from the French words for 'velvet' and 'hook'. [[5]] Its big break came when astronauts used it to stop equipment floating away inside their spacecraft.

Today, Velcro is used on shoes, bags, blood pressure cuffs and even in spacesuits. [[6]] It is a reminder that great ideas can come from paying attention to things that most people would simply brush away.

bank.A: He was curious about how they stuck so firmly.
bank.B: He saw that each one was covered in tiny hooks.
bank.C: One side would have hooks, and the other side would have soft loops.
bank.D: Eventually he discovered that nylon worked much better.
bank.E: At first, few people were interested in buying it.
bank.F: This kind of copying of nature is now called biomimicry.
bank.G: Dogs need to be brushed often to keep their coats healthy.

passages.title: Sleep
passages.intro: Read the four short texts about sleep. For questions 26–33, choose which text (A, B, C or D) each statement matches. You can use each letter more than once.
passages.credit: Original texts written for this practice test. The product in text C is invented.

A.title: Half Asleep (a science article)
A.text: Some animals have remarkable ways of sleeping. Dolphins rest one half of their brain at a time, so the other half can keep them breathing and watching for danger. Many birds can do the same, sleeping with one eye open. Giraffes, which are at risk from predators when lying down, often sleep for only a few minutes at a time. Scientists are still investigating exactly why all animals seem to need sleep at all.

B.title: Summer Nights (a memoir)
B.text: When I was a girl, the summers were so hot that we dragged our mattresses onto the back verandah. My brother and I lay awake listening to the possums thumping on the roof and the frogs in the dam. Mum said we would never get to sleep with all that noise. She was wrong. I have never slept so well since.

C.title: CloudRest Pillows (an advertisement)
C.text: Tired of tossing and turning? The CloudRest pillow is scientifically designed to give you the deepest sleep of your life. Made from our secret blend of foam, it moulds perfectly to your head and neck. Thousands of happy customers can't be wrong! Order today and wake up feeling like a brand-new person.

D.title: Night Shift (a nurse's diary)
D.text: 3 am. The ward is quiet except for the beeping of machines. Most people are fast asleep, but for me this is the middle of the working day. I check on Mr Lim, who can't sleep either, and we talk quietly about cricket until his eyes start to close. Tomorrow I'll sleep while everyone else is at work or school. It's a strange, upside-down life, but I like being awake when the world needs looking after.

questions.stem: The stuffed owl 'regarded visitors with a disapproving, slightly cross-eyed stare' (paragraph 1). What is the effect of this description?

options.A: It shows that the owl is still alive.
options.B: It explains why Nell is frightened of birds.
options.C: It shows that the house is very dark.
options.D: It adds humour while showing how strict and unwelcoming the house feels.

questions.explanation: 'Disapproving' makes the owl seem like a strict grown-up, matching the rules of the house, while 'slightly cross-eyed' makes it funny.

distractors.A: it is stuffed; the description is playful
distractors.C: the description is about the owl's look, not the light

questions.stem: Nell thinks exploring without disturbing anything is 'like swimming without getting wet' (paragraph 2). What does she mean?

options.A: She would rather go swimming than explore.
options.B: The rule is almost impossible to follow.
options.C: The house is damp and cold.

questions.explanation: You can't swim without getting wet, so Nell is saying you can't really explore without touching or moving things: the rule is impossible.

distractors.C: it's not about dampness
distractors.D: she thinks the rule is unreasonable, not that she is careful

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, 'impeccably well-behaved' means

options.A: behaving perfectly, without a single mistake.
options.B: behaving badly but not getting caught.
options.C: behaving well only when someone was watching.
options.D: behaving in a bored, unhappy way.

questions.explanation: 'Impeccably' means perfectly or flawlessly. For two days Nell followed every rule.

distractors.C: the word doesn't suggest pretending
distractors.D: the word is about how well she behaved, not how she felt

questions.stem: The attic stairs 'complained loudly at every step' (paragraph 4). This tells us that the stairs

options.C: creaked noisily, as if they didn't want Nell to climb them.

questions.explanation: Stairs can't really complain. The personification describes loud creaking, and it adds to the feeling that Nell is somewhere she shouldn't be.

distractors.D: the description is about sound, not size

questions.stem: Why does Nell's face 'burn' in paragraph 5?

options.B: She is angry with her great-aunt.
options.C: She feels embarrassed and guilty at being caught.
options.D: She has a fever from the rain.

questions.explanation: She has broken the rule about not disturbing anything, and her great-aunt has caught her: a burning face shows embarrassment and guilt.

distractors.A: the burning is a reaction, not the temperature
distractors.B: she spins round in fright, not anger
distractors.D: nothing about illness

questions.skill: Understanding a change in a character
questions.stem: How does Great-Aunt Harriet change at the end of the story?

options.A: She becomes angrier because Nell disobeyed her.
options.B: She decides to send Nell home.
options.C: She forgets that Nell broke the rules and goes to bed.
options.D: She becomes warmer and more open after remembering her own childhood.

questions.explanation: She smiles 'for the first time', remembers making the drawings at Nell's age, and offers to show Nell Saturn: the strict great-aunt softens and shares something she loves.

distractors.C: she makes a plan for that night

questions.stem: Gap 1: choose the best word.

options.C: useless

questions.explanation: It was difficult to see things in the dark.

distractors.C: 'useless to see' doesn't fit
distractors.D: 'careful to see' isn't English here

questions.stem: Gap 2: choose the best word.

options.C: hardly

questions.explanation: 'Greatly improve' means improve a lot.

distractors.C: hardly means almost not
distractors.D: rarely means not often

questions.stem: Gap 3: choose the best word.

options.C: spilling

questions.explanation: His headlights were 'shining' in the cat's eyes: light shines.

distractors.C: liquids spill, not light

questions.stem: Gap 4: choose the best word.

options.C: studs

questions.explanation: Cat's eyes are small 'studs' set into the road surface.

distractors.D: beads are threaded on string

questions.stem: Gap 5: choose the best word.

options.C: innocent

questions.explanation: 'Ingenious' means very clever and original: simple but ingenious.

distractors.A: an ingredient is part of a recipe
distractors.C: innocent means not guilty
distractors.D: inexpensive means cheap; 'simple but cheap' is not a contrast

questions.stem: Gap 6: choose the best word.

options.C: made

questions.explanation: 'Helped drivers to find their way' is correct and natural.

distractors.B: 'let drivers to find' isn't correct English
distractors.C: 'made drivers to find' isn't correct English
distractors.D: 'kept drivers to find' doesn't make sense

questions.stem: Gap 7: choose the best word.

options.C: repeated

questions.explanation: 'Regarded as' means thought of as.

distractors.C: repeated means done again

questions.stem: Gap 8: choose the best word.

options.C: value

questions.explanation: 'One of the most valuable inventions': an adjective is needed after 'most'.

distractors.C: a noun
distractors.D: a person who values things

questions.stem: Where is the speaker of the poem?

options.A: standing in a meadow, watching a train go past
options.B: riding a horse beside the railway
options.C: inside a moving train, looking out of the window

questions.explanation: The title is 'From a Railway Carriage', and everything outside seems to rush past ('Painted stations whistle by'), which is how it looks from a moving train.

distractors.A: the sights move past the speaker, not the train
distractors.B: the horses are in the meadows, not ridden
distractors.D: the stations 'whistle by', so the speaker isn't waiting

questions.stem: How does the rhythm of the poem help the reader imagine the journey?

options.A: The quick, regular beat sounds like the wheels of a train rushing along.
options.B: The slow, long lines make the journey seem boring.
options.C: The poem has no pattern, like a bumpy road.
options.D: The rhythm stops and starts like a train arriving at stations.

questions.explanation: Lines like 'Faster than fairies, faster than witches' have a fast, galloping, repeated beat, like train wheels clattering over the tracks.

distractors.B: the lines are quick and lively
distractors.C: the poem has a strong regular rhythm and rhyme
distractors.D: the rhythm keeps rushing on

questions.stem: The sights 'Fly as thick as driving rain' (line 6). This suggests that

options.A: so many things rush past so quickly that they blur together.
options.B: it is raining heavily during the journey.
options.C: birds are flying beside the train.
options.D: the window is dirty and hard to see through.

questions.explanation: Driving rain falls thick and fast. The sights pass in the same way: too many, too quickly to take in one by one.

distractors.C: 'fly' describes the sights rushing past, not birds
distractors.D: nothing about a dirty window

questions.stem: In the second stanza, the speaker repeats 'Here is…' and 'there is…'. What is the effect?

options.A: It shows that the train has stopped so the speaker can look around.
options.B: It shows that the speaker is pointing out places on a map.
options.C: It shows that the speaker is bored and repeating himself.
options.D: It gives a quick list of separate snapshots, each seen for only a moment.

questions.explanation: Each 'Here is…' introduces a new picture (a child, a tramp, a cart, a mill), like snapshots flashing past the window one after another.

distractors.A: the sights are 'a glimpse and gone', so the train is still moving
distractors.C: the tone is excited, not bored

questions.stem: What does the last line, 'Each a glimpse and gone for ever!', suggest?

options.A: The speaker is sad that the journey is over.
options.B: Every sight is seen for just a moment and will never be seen again.
options.C: The speaker has lost something out of the window.

questions.explanation: A glimpse is a very quick look. Because the train moves so fast, each sight appears for an instant and is gone, which makes the journey exciting and a little wistful.

distractors.A: the journey is still going on
distractors.C: nothing has been lost
distractors.D: the sights are left behind, not destroyed
